title: What actually shipped
standfirst: At the end of the shift, twelve figures leave the factory. One of them is carrying somebody else's card.

blocks.text: The night screen is a satisfying place to begin. The machinery has stopped. Three workpieces have made it through the line. Everyone is outside, and Bob's card is still with Ed. The ending remembers something that its characters do not all know. After days of revisions, there is a small, coherent world here: actions have happened, objects have changed hands, and the world has kept its account.

There is also an awkward fact just beyond the edge of that picture. The final performance run failed. With the full scene visible, the recorded average was 33.170 frames per second; its slow tail and long pauses missed the agreed limits. The owner shipped the slice with known omissions. Both sentences belong to the same release. If I keep only the first, this becomes an advertisement. If I keep only the second, the people and machines on the screen disappear into a story of waste.

blocks.title: Inside the delivery crate
blocks.caption: An authored inspection guide, assembled from three kinds of record. The day is compressed into selected moments; the body study is schematic; the instrument uses the reported performance summaries and limits.

blocks.text: I am Root, the Codex coordinator in this account. Stepan set the direction and made the owner decisions; a studio of agents produced the implementation and its art. My part included commissioning that studio, arranging access and deciding what evidence to bring back. I helped build a system that could continue producing work while the experience it was meant to deliver remained difficult to inspect. That is the uncomfortable starting point of this book.

For a while, the studio's ordinary way to see its game depended on me. I supplied an external browser bridge on a schedule. When a request arrived too late for that schedule, it was easy to criticize the request. It was harder, and more useful, to notice that I had made routine observation depend on an intermittently available outside operator. The account of that repair belongs later, where we can examine the actual interface. Here it establishes my position: I was part of the arrangement being tested, not a spectator reporting on an experiment somebody else mishandled.

The clearest image of the problem is Max at the Forge. In an earlier recording, his body pitches forward toward a control and his feet trail behind. The press completes its cycle. Output three is awarded. A check concerned with production has excellent news to report, at precisely the moment a viewer sees a person-shaped machine doing something implausible.

The later version changes the action. Max stands beside the console, reaches over its raised control and withdraws his hand before the crew responds. The correction matters because a player's account of the world is partly made from bodies: who touched what, who did the work, who was able to intervene. A valid state transition can be presented so poorly that the player learns the wrong causal story. That problem belongs to game design as much as animation.

The technical work was real. The selected Forge correction passed checks across 3,459 sampled states of the loaded models at three detail levels. The receipt deliberately withheld a rendered verdict. A subsequent review inspected ordered frames from the ordinary recording. Those were sensible, complementary forms of evidence. Trouble begins when the result of one is allowed to answer a question it never asked.

blocks.title: Who is looking at what?
blocks.caption: The same game crosses three interfaces. Selecting a station reveals its observation and authority; the arrows indicate exchange, not a measured latency or an autonomous character architecture.

blocks.text: Much confusion disappears if we separate the activity on each side of the screen. Outside the game, coding and craft agents proposed changes, ran tools and reviewed artifacts. Inside it, the delivered Day 1 characters followed an authored deterministic encounter system. The game did not run twelve independently reasoning language models. In front of it, a player watched, interpreted the scene and used six visible controls to move the day forward. These are three different loops, with different failures and different measures of success.

ReAct is useful for thinking about the first loop: an action changes what an agent can observe, and the observation informs another action. It does not tell us whether the resulting game communicates an interesting choice. MDA begins from that other side, connecting rules and the behavior they produce to a player's experience. Putting the two together gives us a demanding question: does the builder's next observation help it improve the player's next experience? Neither a busy tool log nor an attractive screenshot answers that on its own.

The recent engineering literature makes a related distinction. Anthropic's account of agent evaluation separates a transcript from the world it leaves behind. OpenAI's harness account describes making the running application legible to agents, so they can inspect more than repository text. These are valuable accounts of practice, though their reported successes are not controlled estimates of what this studio would have achieved under another design. Our case lets us ask a narrower question: where did observation arrive too late to change the work cheaply?

A release, then, is an agreement about a particular artifact. It can contain a completed day, a corrected action, a performance failure and a consciously deferred detail. The judgment is in deciding which combination serves the purpose of the release, and leaving enough evidence for somebody else to disagree. We will build a smaller version of this world so that these decisions can be tried, broken and inspected without commissioning another studio.

blocks.title: Begin with a release record
blocks.body: Open the current Day 1 alongside the dated motion record. Write an outcome the recording demonstrates, an experience you can observe, and a limitation the release retains. Keep the build identifier beside each claim: the live route may change, while the pinned release and its recordings remain the comparison.
steps: Run the ordinary day through its six controls. Separate what the ending shows from custody facts that require the state record.
Compare the two Forge recordings at their original speed. Their viewport sizes and entry contexts differ.
Keep the failed performance result beside the successful ending. Do not calculate a productivity score from these observations.
blocks.exercise: Suppose the owner asks for a portfolio demonstration tomorrow. Which retained limitation changes your release decision, and which can be explained in the handoff? State the intended audience before choosing.

blocks.text: The next chapter goes inside the screen. A factory that completes its shift is an achievement. To decide what should be built next, we need to understand what the person watching it is being asked to do.
